title: Web3 Community Analysis & Authentic Engagement Guide
subtitle: Learn to Evaluate Community Health and Detect Fake Activity

intro.title: Introduction: Community as Moat
intro.content:
In Web3, community isn't just a marketing channel—it's your competitive moat. While code can be forked and products can be copied, a strong, engaged community is nearly impossible to replicate.

But here's the problem: Community size is easy to fake. You can buy 50,000 Discord members for $500. You can hire bots to spam Telegram chats. You can coordinate raid groups to inflate engagement metrics.

This guide teaches you to see through the noise. You'll learn to distinguish between authentic communities that drive real value and fake communities that exist only on dashboards. Whether you're evaluating a project to invest in or building your own community, these skills are essential.

discord_analysis.title: Discord Community Analysis
discord_analysis.content: Discord is the primary hub for Web3 communities. But member count tells you almost nothing. A server with 100,000 members might have only 500 active users—or worse, 90% bots.

member_metrics.title: Real Member Count vs Total Members
member_metrics.content:
The total member count you see is meaningless. What matters is DAU (Daily Active Users) and MAU (Monthly Active Users).

How to check:

  • Look at the member list at different times of day
  • Count how many members are showing as "online" during peak hours
  • A healthy ratio: 5-15% of total members online during peak times
  • Check the "Members" sidebar during UTC peak hours (14:00-20:00)

Benchmark metrics:

  • 10,000 members, 500-1,500 online = Healthy
  • 10,000 members, 50-200 online = Dead or fake
  • New projects: 20-30% online ratio is common (still small, engaged)
  • Mature projects: 5-10% online ratio is normal

Red flag: Member count jumps by thousands overnight but online count stays the same = Bought members

activity_patterns.title: Message Velocity and Quality
activity_patterns.content:
Message volume matters less than message quality and distribution.

Healthy activity patterns:

  • Message timing: Spread throughout the day across timezones (global community)
  • Message length: Mix of short responses and detailed discussions
  • Channel distribution: Activity across multiple channels, not just #general
  • Conversation depth: Multi-message threads, questions get answered
  • User diversity: Different usernames in conversations (not the same 5 people)

Unhealthy patterns:

  • All messages in one 30-minute window = Coordinated shilling
  • Only emoji reactions, no substantive replies = Bot engagement
  • Messages only in #announcements = One-way broadcast, no community
  • Same users posting repeatedly = Small group creating fake activity

Tool check: Use Discord's search function to find messages from the past week. Healthy communities should have 500+ unique participants in a 10k member server.

bot_detection.title: Detecting Bots and Fake Engagement
bot_detection.content:
Bot detection requires examining user profiles and behavior patterns.

Bot profile characteristics:

  • Generic usernames: user12345, crypto_fan_8392
  • Default avatars: No custom profile picture
  • New accounts: Account created within days of joining server
  • No activity history: Joined but never posted
  • Identical join times: Hundreds of users joined within same hour

Bot behavior patterns:

  • Generic messages: "Great project!", "To the moon!", "LFG!"
  • Immediate reactions to announcements (within seconds, hundreds of reactions)
  • Copy-pasted messages across multiple servers
  • No follow-up when asked questions

How to test:

  1. Click on 20 random "online" members
  2. Check their join dates and account creation dates
  3. Look at their message history in the server
  4. If 50%+ are brand new accounts with no messages = Bot farm

Welcome bot indicators: If every new member is greeted with identical messages from different accounts within 1 minute = Coordinated bot greeting (meant to fake activity)

role_distribution.title: Role Distribution Analysis
role_distribution.content:
Role structure reveals a lot about community organization and engagement.

Healthy role distribution:

  • Active contributor roles: 5-15% of members have earned roles through participation
  • OG/Early supporter: 1-5% (shows long-term community)
  • Moderators: 1 mod per 500-1000 active members
  • Verified roles: Users who completed onboarding/verification
  • Specialized roles: Developers, artists, ambassadors with actual activity

Red flags:

  • 90% of members have no role = No engagement system or fake members
  • Everyone has "OG" role = Meaningless, likely given to all to inflate ego
  • Too many moderators (1 mod per 50 members) = Trying to create appearance of structure
  • Complex role hierarchy with no clear earning criteria = Vanity system

Channel activity by role: Check if role holders actually participate. In healthy communities, users with contributor roles should be visible in recent messages.

telegram_analysis.title: Telegram Community Analysis
telegram_analysis.content: Telegram is even easier to manipulate than Discord. Member counts are almost always inflated. Focus entirely on message patterns and admin quality.

authenticity_checking.title: Member Authenticity
authenticity_checking.content:
Telegram doesn't show "online" status, making it harder to gauge real activity. You must rely on participation metrics.

Participation ratio formula:

  • Take total member count
  • Count unique message senders in past 7 days
  • Healthy ratio: 2-5% of members actively message weekly
  • Elite communities: 10-20% weekly participation
  • Dead/fake: <0.5% participation

Example: 20,000 member group with 100 unique weekly senders = 0.5% = Mostly dead or fake

How to check unique senders:

  1. Scroll through recent messages
  2. Count distinct usernames over past week
  3. Compare to total member count
  4. Tools like Combot can provide analytics if enabled

Profile checking:

  • Click 10 random members
  • Check if they have profile photos
  • Check last seen status (if visible)
  • Accounts with no photo + "last seen long time ago" = Inactive or fake

message_patterns.title: Message Patterns and Timing
message_patterns.content:
Authentic communities have organic conversation flow. Fake communities have suspicious patterns.

Organic patterns:

  • Varied message timing: Activity throughout the day
  • Conversation threads: Questions get answers, discussions develop
  • Mixed content: Links, questions, discussions, memes, reactions
  • Natural language: Different writing styles, languages, emojis

Fake patterns:

  • Burst activity: 100 messages in 5 minutes, then silence for hours
  • Shill waves: Coordinated positive messages during announcements
  • Copy-paste: Identical or very similar messages from multiple accounts
  • Unnatural enthusiasm: Every message extremely positive with moon emojis
  • No questions: Healthy communities ask questions; shills don't

Time zone test: Check activity during off-peak hours (3-6 AM UTC). If group is "global" but has zero messages during these hours, it's likely concentrated shilling (possibly same timezone, coordinated team).

admin_responsiveness.title: Admin Activity and Responsiveness
admin_responsiveness.content:
Active, responsive admins are the strongest signal of a healthy community.

What to check:

  • Response time: How long until legitimate questions get admin responses?
  • Response quality: Do admins give detailed answers or generic responses?
  • Admin presence: Do admins participate in discussions beyond announcements?
  • Multiple admins: Are there multiple active admins across timezones?

Healthy admin behavior:

  • Questions answered within 1-6 hours
  • Admins engage in casual conversation, not just announcements
  • Clear rules and enforcement (spam/scams removed quickly)
  • Transparency about issues and delays
  • Different admins active at different times (timezone coverage)

Red flags:

  • No admin responses for days = Abandoned or hired community managers
  • Only post announcements, never answer questions = Broadcasting, not community building
  • Delete all critical questions = Censorship, hiding problems
  • Overly defensive responses = Team insecurity
  • Single admin active 24/7 = Likely bot or hired CM with no real connection

spam_detection.title: Spam and Scam Detection
spam_detection.content:
Unmoderated spam is a huge red flag. It means either the admins don't care or the group is entirely fake.

Types of spam in Telegram:

  • Scam links: Fake websites impersonating the project
  • Pump groups: Invitations to pump-and-dump schemes
  • Competitor shilling: Other projects being promoted
  • Airdrop scams: "Connect your wallet to claim"
  • Impersonator DMs: Fake admins DMing users (real admins never DM first)

Moderation quality test:

  1. Look for obvious spam in recent messages
  2. Check how long spam stays up before deletion
  3. Good moderation: Spam deleted within minutes
  4. Poor moderation: Spam stays for hours or days
  5. No moderation: Spam everywhere = Dead group or scam

Bot protection: Healthy groups use bots to prevent spam (CaptchaBot, anti-spam bots). If there's no bot protection and no spam, the group is either very small or fake (real groups always attract spam).

fake_communities.title: Detecting Fake Communities
fake_communities.content: Fake communities are everywhere in Web3. They're designed to create the illusion of popularity and legitimacy. Here's how to spot them.

bought_members.title: Signs of Bought Members
bought_members.content:
Buying members is trivially easy and cheap. Here are the telltale signs:

Obvious indicators:

  • Sudden spikes: +5,000 members overnight with no major announcement
  • Dead members: High member count but <1% online
  • New accounts: Most members joined Discord/Telegram recently (within weeks)
  • Generic profiles: Default avatars, numbered usernames, no bios
  • Zero activity: Thousands of members, but <50 messages per day

Member growth analysis:

  • Organic growth: Gradual, correlates with announcements, partnerships, product launches
  • Bought growth: Sudden, unexplained jumps with no corresponding external activity

Price comparison (for reference):

  • 1,000 Discord members: $10-20
  • 10,000 Discord members: $100-200
  • 1,000 Telegram members: $5-10
  • Services: Search "buy Discord members" and you'll find dozens

How to verify: Ask project team about their growth strategy. Legitimate projects can explain growth (marketing campaign, partnership announcement, product launch). Projects with bought members can't explain the spikes.

manipulation_tactics.title: Engagement Manipulation Tactics
manipulation_tactics.content:
Beyond buying members, there are many tactics to fake engagement:

Paid shilling:

  • Hire people to post positive messages on schedule
  • Pay for reactions to every announcement within seconds
  • Coordinate "organic" discussions that are actually scripted
  • Cost: $500-2000/month for small team of shills

Raid groups:

  • Organize group to join competitor channels and shill your project
  • Coordinate mass voting on polls to appear more popular
  • Brigade social media posts with positive comments
  • Easy to spot: Same accounts appear across multiple projects doing same behavior

Sock puppet accounts:

  • Team members create multiple fake accounts
  • Use these accounts to ask softball questions in AMAs
  • Manufacture "community demand" for features team already planned
  • Detection: Similar writing styles, posting patterns, always defensive of project

Announcement manipulation:

  • Post minor updates as "major announcements" to create activity
  • Re-announce old news to different audiences
  • Coordinate team to react immediately (creating false urgency)

Vanity metrics gaming:

  • Host "engagement" contests that require likes/shares (buying engagement with prizes)
  • Give special roles for inviting members (pyramid scheme dynamics)
  • Create dozens of sub-channels to appear organized (but all are dead)

ghost_town_indicators.title: Ghost Town Detection
ghost_town_indicators.content:
A "ghost town" is a community with high member count but zero real activity. These are usually bought communities that were never nurtured.

Ghost town characteristics:

  • High members, low messages: 50,000 members but <100 messages/day
  • One-way communication: Only admins post, no community replies
  • Ancient messages: Scroll to recent messages, see timestamps from days ago
  • No reactions: Announcements get zero or very few reactions
  • Empty voice channels: Discord has voice/stage channels but never used
  • Dead events: Community events posted but no one shows up

Activity degradation pattern:

  1. Project launches with real early community (100-1000 members)
  2. Growth stalls, team buys members to appear successful
  3. New members are fake, don't participate
  4. Real members leave due to lack of real community
  5. Eventually only bought members remain = Ghost town

The ratio test:

  • Healthy: 1 message per 10 members per day (10k members = 1000 msgs/day)
  • Acceptable: 1 message per 50 members per day (10k members = 200 msgs/day)
  • Ghost town: 1 message per 500+ members per day (10k members = <20 msgs/day)

case_studies.title: Case Studies of Exposed Fake Communities
case_studies.content:
Real examples of projects caught with fake communities:

Case Study 1: The 300K Member Scam

A 2023 DeFi project claimed 300,000 Discord members and "massive community support." Investigation revealed:

  • Member accounts created in bulk, same day as join date
  • Only 400-600 members online at any time (<0.2%)
  • Investigation by community members found the same member IDs across 50+ other scam projects
  • Project rugged 2 months later, $4M stolen

Case Study 2: The Shill Army

An NFT project in 2022 had extremely active Twitter and Discord presence. But:

  • Same 20 accounts appeared in every discussion
  • These accounts had similar writing style and timing
  • When confronted, all accounts went silent simultaneously
  • Team later admitted to hiring offshore engagement team for $1000/month

Case Study 3: The Raid Group

Multiple projects in 2021 used the same raid group service:

  • 100+ accounts would join Discord, post enthusiastic messages
  • After 48 hours, accounts would leave
  • Same accounts appeared across dozens of failed projects
  • Service cost: $500 per raid, guaranteed 100+ messages in 24 hours

What happened: All three projects failed. Fake communities don't convert to real users, revenue, or long-term success. They only fool naive investors temporarily.

healthy_metrics.title: Healthy Community Metrics
healthy_metrics.content: Now that you know what fake looks like, let's establish what healthy communities actually measure and optimize for.

retention_rates.title: Retention and Churn Rates
retention_rates.content:
Retention is the single most important community metric. Growth means nothing if everyone leaves.

How to measure retention:

  • 30-day retention: Of users who joined 30 days ago, what % are still active?
  • 90-day retention: Long-term engagement indicator
  • Active to total ratio: Monthly active users / Total members

Benchmark retention rates:

  • Excellent: 40-60% 30-day retention
  • Good: 20-40% 30-day retention
  • Average: 10-20% 30-day retention
  • Poor: <10% 30-day retention

How communities track this: Discord bots like MEE6, Statbot can track member join/leave dates and activity. Premium analytics tools provide retention dashboards.

Churn analysis:

  • Healthy churn: Users leave gradually over months as interests change
  • Unhealthy churn: Mass exodus after specific events (rug pull fears, team controversy)
  • Check member count history: If it only goes up, they're likely counting inactive/bought members

What to ask project teams: "What's your 30-day retention rate?" Most teams don't track this. Teams that do are serious about community health.

onboarding_quality.title: New Member Onboarding
onboarding_quality.content:
The first experience sets the tone. Good communities have intentional onboarding; bad ones just have welcome bots.

High-quality onboarding indicators:

  • Clear introduction flow: New members know where to start, what to read first
  • Verification process: Captcha or simple questions to prevent bots
  • Welcome channel: Active responses from real members (not just bots)
  • Onboarding guides: Written guides or videos explaining community structure
  • Early engagement prompts: "Introduce yourself", "What brought you here?"
  • Helper roles: Designated community members help new users

Poor onboarding signs:

  • No clear starting point, new members confused
  • Welcome bot message, then silence
  • Immediately hit with rules/restrictions (hostile vibe)
  • Forced to "verify" by visiting external links (scam)
  • No response when new members ask questions

The 10-minute test: Join a community as a new member. In 10 minutes, can you:

  1. Understand what the project does?
  2. Know where to ask questions?
  3. Get a response from a real person?

If no to any = Poor onboarding = Poor community health

user_content.title: User-Generated Content Ratio
user_content.content:
Healthy communities create their own content. They don't just passively consume official announcements.

Types of user-generated content:

  • Educational threads explaining concepts
  • Memes and artwork related to the project
  • Tutorial videos and guides
  • Community-organized events and initiatives
  • Third-party tools and dashboards
  • Research and analysis posts
  • Translation to other languages

Content ratio benchmark:

  • Healthy: 60-80% of content is user-generated
  • Acceptable: 40-60% user-generated
  • Poor: <20% user-generated (mostly official announcements)

How to assess:

  1. Scroll through recent Discord messages or Telegram posts
  2. Count how many are from team vs community
  3. Check if community members share external content (articles, tutorials)
  4. Look for channels dedicated to community creations

Content quality signals:

  • Community members cite specific features/documentation (they actually use the product)
  • Debates about product direction (engaged enough to care)
  • Users helping each other without team intervention
  • Organic discussions unrelated to token price

Red flag: The only content is price speculation and "wen moon" memes = No real product engagement

governance_participation.title: Governance Participation Rates
governance_participation.content:
For DAO-governed projects, governance participation is the ultimate test of community engagement.

Governance metrics to check:

  • Voter turnout: % of token holders who vote on proposals
  • Proposal quality: Are proposals well-researched or low-effort?
  • Discussion depth: Do proposals get debated before voting?
  • Voter distribution: Is voting power concentrated or distributed?

Benchmark participation rates:

  • Excellent: >20% token holder participation
  • Good: 10-20% participation
  • Average: 5-10% participation
  • Poor: <5% participation (governance is theater)

Where to check: Snapshot.org, on-chain governance contracts, project's governance forum (Discourse, Commonwealth)

Quality over quantity:

  • Small DAOs with 20% participation > Large DAOs with 2% participation
  • Check if the same whales vote on everything (centralization)
  • Read proposal discussions: Are they substantive or just "yes/no"?

Red flags:

  • Proposals pass with <5% turnout = Community doesn't care
  • All proposals pass 99%+ = Rubber stamp governance, not real
  • No discussion before votes = Community doesn't understand proposals
  • Team controls >50% voting power = Governance is fake

cross_platform.title: Cross-Platform Engagement Correlation
cross_platform.content:
Authentic communities are engaged across multiple platforms. Fake communities have inconsistent engagement patterns.

Platforms to compare:

  • Discord server activity
  • Telegram group activity
  • Twitter/X followers and engagement
  • Forum/Reddit discussions
  • GitHub activity (for open-source projects)
  • Governance platform participation

Correlation test: Do the activity levels make sense together?

Healthy correlation examples:

  • 10k Discord members, 8k Twitter followers, 500 governance voters = Consistent
  • 50k Discord, 40k Telegram, 100k Twitter, 2k active discussers = Reasonable funnel

Red flag combinations:

  • 100k Discord, 5k Twitter followers = Discord bought, Twitter organic
  • 50k Twitter followers, 100 Discord members = Twitter bought or project dead
  • High social media, zero GitHub activity for "open source" = Vaporware
  • High member counts, zero governance participation = Fake community

Engagement rate consistency:

  • Check Twitter engagement rate (replies, retweets per tweet)
  • Compare to Discord activity level
  • Similar engagement quality across platforms = Real community
  • High numbers but low engagement everywhere = All fake

The authenticity test: Real communities cluster around the product. If Discord is active but no one uses the actual product (check on-chain metrics, app downloads) = Mercenary community only there for airdrops.

building_communities.title: Building Authentic Communities (For Builders)
building_communities.content: If you're building a Web3 project, here's how to build a real community that becomes your competitive advantage.

community_first.title: Community-First vs Token-First Approach
community_first.content:
The fundamental choice: Build community around shared values and product, or around speculation and token price.

Community-first approach:

  • Start with a small group of true believers (10-100 people)
  • Focus on product-market fit before growing community
  • Give early community real influence on product direction
  • Grow slowly through authentic value creation
  • Token (if any) comes after community is established

Token-first approach (usually fails):

  • Launch token before product
  • Focus on price speculation to attract members
  • Rapid growth through marketing and hype
  • Community only cares about token value
  • Price drops → community disappears

Examples of community-first success:

  • Ethereum: Built community of developers for years before token launch
  • Uniswap: Product worked, community formed organically, token airdropped to users later
  • ENS: Years of product development, then retroactive airdrop to community

Why community-first wins:

  • Members have aligned values beyond money
  • Community stays during bear markets
  • Real users provide better product feedback
  • Word-of-mouth growth is sustainable
  • Community becomes defensible moat

Start small, stay small longer: Don't rush to 10k members. 100 engaged members > 10,000 lurkers.

moderation.title: Moderation Best Practices
moderation.content:
Good moderation creates safe space for authentic community to thrive. Poor moderation leads to spam, scams, and toxic culture.

Moderation structure:

  • Ratio: 1 active moderator per 500-1000 active members (not total members)
  • Timezone coverage: Mods across different timezones for 24/7 coverage
  • Clear hierarchy: Junior mods, senior mods, community managers, team members
  • Specialized mods: Technical support, partnerships, events, etc.

Essential moderation rules:

  • Zero tolerance: Scams, impersonation, spam (immediate ban)
  • Strict limits: Price speculation confined to specific channel
  • No toxicity: Personal attacks, harassment, racism, sexism = ban
  • No shilling: Other projects can't be promoted (exception: partners)
  • Helpful environment: No question is stupid, newbies welcomed

Moderation transparency:

  • Public mod log showing bans and reasons
  • Appeal process for unfair bans
  • Mod guidelines publicly documented
  • Regular mod feedback sessions with community

What NOT to do:

  • Don't delete all criticism (creates echo chamber)
  • Don't let mods abuse power (lost community trust)
  • Don't over-moderate (kills organic discussion)
  • Don't under-moderate (spam takes over)

Bot-assisted moderation: Use bots for automated spam filtering, but always have human mods for nuanced situations.

incentive_design.title: Incentive Design Without Gaming
incentive_design.content:
Incentives drive behavior. Design them well and you get valuable contributions. Design them poorly and you get gaming and mercenaries.

Good incentive designs:

  • Reward actual value: Quality content, helpful answers, bug reports, translations
  • Make it hard to game: Manual review, qualitative criteria, peer voting
  • Long-term alignment: Vesting periods, ongoing contribution requirements
  • Recognize non-financial value: Recognition, exclusive access, governance power

Examples of well-designed incentives:

  • Bug bounties: Pay for security vulnerabilities (valuable, hard to fake)
  • Content creation: Reward quality tutorials, guides, translations (reviewed by community)
  • Ambassador programs: Local community leaders get support + recognition
  • Contributor roles: Earned through consistent participation over time
  • Retroactive rewards: Reward past contributions without announcement (prevents gaming)

Bad incentive designs (avoid):

  • Pay per invite: Creates spam, fake members, pyramid dynamics
  • Pay per message: Creates spam, low-quality content
  • Pay per reaction: Creates fake engagement, bot farms
  • Automatic rewards: No quality check = gaming

The gaming test: Before launching an incentive, ask: "How would I game this if I wanted to extract maximum value with minimum effort?" If the answer is easy, redesign.

Balance: Some members contribute for rewards, others for passion. Design for both. Don't make everything transactional (kills intrinsic motivation) but don't expect everyone to work for free.

scaling_culture.title: Scaling Without Losing Culture
scaling_culture.content:
The hardest challenge: Growing from 100 to 10,000 members without losing the magic that made the first 100 special.

Culture preservation strategies:

  • Document culture early: Write down your values, norms, what makes your community unique
  • Onboarding enculturation: Teach new members the culture, not just the rules
  • Recognize culture carriers: Identify members who embody your values, make them examples
  • Smaller sub-groups: Create channels for specialized interests (keeps intimate feel)

Dangerous growth phases:

  • 100 → 1,000: Need formal moderation and structure (informal doesn't scale)
  • 1,000 → 10,000: Risk of eternal September (newcomers overwhelm old culture)
  • 10,000+: Need sub-communities or culture becomes diluted broadcast

Anti-patterns that kill culture:

  • Buying members (they don't share your values)
  • Rapid hyped growth (attracts speculators, not believers)
  • Removing OG members (lose culture carriers)
  • Ignoring culture violations (new members don't learn norms)
  • Over-professionalizing (corporate feel replaces grassroots energy)

Maintaining founder presence: As community grows, founder time becomes scarce. Balance:

  • Regular AMAs and Q&As (stay accessible)
  • Empower community leaders (don't need founder for everything)
  • Pop into discussions occasionally (show you're listening)
  • Write personal updates (maintain human connection)

The fork option: Sometimes it's better to let community fork into multiple sub-communities rather than diluting the original. Ethereum → Bitcoin culture split is an example.

due_diligence.title: Community Due Diligence Checklist
due_diligence.content: Before investing time or money in a Web3 project, perform community due diligence. Here's your systematic process.

quick_assessment.title: 10-Minute Quick Assessment
quick_assessment.content:
First pass filter to eliminate obvious fakes and low-quality communities.

Step 1: Member count reality check (2 min)

  • Join Discord server
  • Check total members vs online members
  • Expected ratio: 5-15% online during peak hours
  • If <2% online → Likely fake or dead

Step 2: Recent activity scan (3 min)

  • Scroll through general chat last 24 hours
  • Count unique message senders
  • Check if conversations have depth (multi-message threads)
  • If <20 unique senders in 24h for 10k+ member server → Red flag

Step 3: Profile spot check (2 min)

  • Click 10 random online members
  • Check join dates, account ages, avatars
  • If >50% have default avatars + new accounts → Bot farm

Step 4: Admin presence check (2 min)

  • Search for recent messages from team/admins
  • Check if they're answering questions or just posting announcements
  • Look for admin activity in past 7 days
  • No admin activity or only announcements → Poor community management

Step 5: Cross-platform consistency (1 min)

  • Check Twitter follower count
  • Compare to Discord member count
  • Check follower engagement (replies to tweets)
  • Major discrepancy (10x difference) → Something is bought

Decision point: If project fails 2+ of these quick checks, skip it. Not worth deeper investigation.

deep_dive.title: Deep-Dive Investigation Process
deep_dive.content:
For projects that pass quick assessment and you're seriously considering, do deep investigation.

Phase 1: Historical analysis (30 min)

  • Check Discord member growth over time (tools: Discord analytics bots)
  • Look for suspicious growth spikes
  • Correlation with announcements/partnerships?
  • Check archive.org for website/social media history
  • Did they claim huge community before it existed?

Phase 2: Engagement quality (30 min)

  • Read 100 most recent messages in detail
  • Assess message quality: Are they substantive or just hype?
  • Check for repeated talking points (coordinated shilling)
  • Look at different channels: Is activity spread or concentrated?
  • Search for specific discussions about product features

Phase 3: Member interviews (20 min)

  • DM 3-5 random active members (not team)
  • Ask: "How did you find this project?"
  • Ask: "What do you like about the community?"
  • Ask: "Have you used the product?"
  • Real members give detailed, varied answers
  • Shills/bots give generic or no response

Phase 4: Governance check (15 min, if applicable)

  • Go to Snapshot or governance forum
  • Check recent proposal participation rates
  • Read proposal discussions for quality
  • Check voting power distribution (Gini coefficient)
  • Low participation or extreme centralization → Red flag

Phase 5: External validation (15 min)

  • Search "[project name] fake community" on Twitter
  • Check Reddit for discussions about the project
  • Look for community complaints or exposés
  • Check if team responds to criticism maturely

Total time: ~2 hours for comprehensive due diligence. Worth it if you're considering significant investment.

red_flags.title: Red Flags Summary
red_flags.content:
A comprehensive list of community red flags. Any ONE of these warrants caution. Multiple red flags = stay away.

Membership red flags:

  • Member count jumped >50% overnight with no major announcement
  • Online ratio consistently <2% of total members
  • Majority of members have default avatars
  • Mass join dates (thousands joined same day)
  • Member accounts created same day they joined server

Activity red flags:

  • <1 message per 100 members per day
  • Only activity is in announcement channel
  • Messages only during specific hours (coordinated shilling)
  • Generic positive messages with no substance
  • No questions from community (healthy communities ask lots of questions)

Admin/Team red flags:

  • Admins never answer community questions
  • Delete all critical questions or concerns
  • Defensive/hostile responses to legitimate critique
  • Team members only post announcements, never engage
  • Impossible to contact team outside official channels

Content red flags:

  • 100% of content is official announcements
  • No user-generated content (guides, tutorials, memes)
  • Only discussion topic is token price
  • No technical discussions about product
  • Community can't explain what the product actually does

Governance red flags:

  • <5% participation in governance votes
  • All proposals pass with >95% approval
  • Team controls >50% voting power
  • No discussion before votes (rubber stamp)
  • Governance exists but nothing ever changes

Cross-platform red flags:

  • 10x discrepancy between platform sizes (one is fake)
  • High follower count but low engagement everywhere
  • GitHub inactive for "open-source" project
  • Product metrics don't match community size

Cultural red flags:

  • Cult-like devotion, no criticism allowed
  • Attack anyone who asks hard questions
  • "Us vs them" mentality against all competitors
  • Obsession with price, not product
  • Conspiracy theories about FUD and short sellers

The ultimate red flag: When you ask hard questions and get banned/attacked instead of answers.

dau.definition: The number of unique users who engage with a community platform each day. Much more meaningful than total member count for measuring real engagement.

mau.definition: The number of unique users who engage with a community platform each month. Used to measure sustained engagement over longer periods.

retention_rate.definition: The percentage of users who remain active in a community after a specific time period (e.g., 30-day retention). High retention indicates strong community health.

churn.definition: The rate at which members leave a community. High churn indicates problems with community value or culture.

engagement_rate.definition: The percentage of community members who actively participate (message, react, vote) within a given time period. Key metric for community health.

community_manager.definition: A role responsible for nurturing community growth, facilitating discussions, organizing events, and serving as bridge between team and community.

moderator.definition: Community members with permissions to enforce rules, remove spam/scams, timeout/ban users, and maintain healthy discussion environment.

raid.definition: Coordinated group action where multiple accounts simultaneously join a community to spam, shill, or manipulate perception. Often paid service.

shill.definition: Someone who aggressively promotes a project, often with compensation or coordination. Differs from genuine advocacy by being inauthentic and repetitive.

fud.definition: Negative information or rumors spread to damage a project's reputation. Can be legitimate criticism or coordinated attack. Often used to dismiss valid concerns.

alpha_group.definition: Exclusive community or channel where early/insider information is shared. Can be legitimate (early supporters) or problematic (insider trading).

whale_group.definition: Private community of large token holders who coordinate actions. Can significantly influence governance and token price.

governance_participation.definition: The rate at which token holders vote on protocol proposals. Low participation indicates community apathy or disengagement from project direction.

community_led_growth.definition: Growth strategy where community members drive adoption through authentic advocacy, content creation, and word-of-mouth rather than paid marketing.
